prompt: A fraud dataset is 1% fraud. A model that always predicts 'not fraud' scores 99% accuracy. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: The model is excellent and should be deployed
Accuracy is misleading under class imbalance; precision and recall on the rare class are needed
Fraud detection is impossible
The dataset needs more rows

explanation: With rare positives, 'always no' is accurate and useless: recall on fraud is 0%. Imbalanced problems are judged by precision/recall on the class you care about.

prompt: Why does the test set lose its value each time you use it to guide a modeling decision?

options.text: The file gets corrupted by repeated reads
Your choices gradually overfit to it, so it stops estimating performance on truly unseen data
Test sets legally expire after one use
It doesn't: you should tune on the test set

explanation: Every decision informed by test performance leaks information about the test set into the model. That's the validation set's job; the test set is spent honestly only once.

prompt: Scaling features using the mean and standard deviation of the ENTIRE dataset before splitting causes…

options.text: …no problem; statistics are just numbers
…preprocessing leakage: test-set statistics influence training, inflating measured performance
…underfitting
…the model to train slower

explanation: Preprocessing must be fit on the training set only and then applied to validation/test. Otherwise information about held-out data flows into training: a subtle but real leak.

prompt: Model A: 99% train / 74% validation. Model B: 82% train / 81% validation. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A is better because its training score is higher
A is overfitting (large generalization gap); B generalizes better and is the one to ship
B is underfitting and must be discarded
Both are equally good

explanation: The 25-point gap is memorization. Unseen-data performance is the only score that matters, and B wins it.

prompt: For time-ordered data (e.g., sales history), the honest split is…

options.text: …random shuffle 80/20
…train on earlier periods, test on the most recent, because production predicts the future from the past
…alphabetical by customer name
…no split; use all data for training

explanation: Evaluation should rehearse deployment. Random splits let the model peek at the future, inflating every metric.

prompt: A model produces 80 true positives, 20 false positives, and 20 false negatives. What is its precision, as a percentage?
explanation: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) = 80/100 = 80%. (Recall here is also 80/100 = 80%.)

prompt: Raising a classifier's decision threshold typically causes…

options.text: …precision to rise and recall to fall
…both precision and recall to rise
…recall to rise and precision to fall
…no change to either

explanation: A stricter bar means alarms fire only on stronger evidence (fewer false alarms → precision up) while weaker true cases are missed (recall down).

prompt: In disease screening, tuning for high recall at the cost of precision is justified because…

options.text: …false positives are more dangerous than false negatives
…a missed case can be fatal while a false alarm costs only a follow-up test
…recall is always the better metric in every domain
…precision cannot be computed for medical data

explanation: Metric choice follows error costs. Screening's asymmetry (deadly FN, cheap FP) favors recall; a payment-blocking system with opposite costs favors precision.

prompt: Your new model beats 'predict last month's value' by 1 percentage point. The most professional response is to…

options.text: …celebrate and deploy immediately
…weigh the permanent pipeline/monitoring cost against the tiny gain, and look for better features before more model complexity
…delete the baseline so the comparison looks better
…double the model size

explanation: A near-baseline result says the signal isn't in your features. Complexity has a permanent operating cost that a one-point edge rarely repays.

prompt: Overall error is 9%; new customers err at 23%, existing at 6%. Why is segment-level error analysis the right next move?

options.text: It lets you delete the bad segment from the test set
It localizes the failure to a population, usually pointing to a fixable data gap (e.g., missing history for new customers)
It always proves the model needs more layers
Aggregates are more honest than breakdowns

explanation: Aggregate metrics hide concentrated failures. Finding where errors cluster generates hypotheses, and data fixes usually beat model fixes.

prompt: Which of the following are forms of leakage? Select all that apply.

options.text: A feature that is a consequence of the label (e.g., collection calls for default prediction)
Random-splitting time-series data
Near-duplicate records appearing in both train and test
Using a validation set to choose hyperparameters

explanation: Target leakage, temporal leakage, and duplicate leakage all inflate scores dishonestly. Using validation for tuning is the validation set's intended job, not leakage.

prompt: For most tabular business data, the strongest default model family is…

options.text: …gradient-boosted tree ensembles
…very deep neural networks
…k-nearest neighbors
…always linear regression, never anything else

explanation: Boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) remain the tabular benchmark to beat. Deep learning dominates unstructured data (images, audio, text) not spreadsheets.

prompt: A model is 'well calibrated' when…

options.text: …its accuracy exceeds 90%
…events it scores at 80% actually occur about 80% of the time
…it runs in under 100 ms
…precision equals recall

explanation: Calibration means scores are trustworthy as probabilities: essential when thresholds, costs, or humans consume the scores downstream.

prompt: K-fold cross-validation exists primarily to…

options.text: …get a more reliable performance estimate from limited data by averaging over several train/validation splits
…train k different production models
…make training k times faster
…replace the test set entirely

explanation: One small validation split is a noisy estimate; k rotations average the noise. The untouched test set still delivers the final honest number.

prompt: For a 1%-positive fraud dataset, which training-time measures address the imbalance?

options.text: Class weights or resampling so the minority class influences the loss, plus evaluation by precision/recall rather than accuracy
Deleting most negative examples from the test set too
Using accuracy but reporting it twice
Nothing; imbalance only affects deep learning

explanation: Weighting/resampling fixes the training signal; metric choice fixes the measurement. Touching the TEST distribution, however, would falsify the evaluation.

prompt: You must pick one number to compare classifiers on an imbalanced task where both false alarms and misses matter. The standard choice is…

options.text: F1: the harmonic mean of precision and recall, which punishes neglecting either
Accuracy
Training loss
Row count

explanation: The harmonic mean collapses to zero if either component does: you can't F1 your way past ignoring one error type. (With asymmetric costs, weighted variants or the raw pair are better still.)

prompt: A churn model uses 'support tickets in the 30 days after the prediction date' as a feature. The problem is…

options.text: …temporal leakage: the feature isn't knowable at prediction time, so offline metrics inflate and production performance collapses
…support tickets are irrelevant to churn
…30 days is too short a window
…nothing; more features always help

explanation: Every feature must pass the 'knowable at prediction moment' test. Future-derived features are answer keys smuggled into training.

prompt: How do you check whether a model's probability outputs are calibrated?

options.text: Bucket predictions by stated probability and compare each bucket's actual outcome rate: the 80% bucket should come true about 80% of the time
Check that probabilities are all above 0.5
Verify the probabilities sum to the row count
Calibration cannot be measured

explanation: A reliability check per confidence bucket. Miscalibrated scores break every threshold and every human decision that consumes them.

prompt: MAE versus RMSE: when does RMSE tell a usefully different story?

options.text: When large individual errors matter disproportionately: RMSE squares errors, so a few big misses dominate it while MAE averages them away
Never; they are always equal
When the data contains categories
Only on GPU hardware

explanation: Choose the metric that mirrors the cost structure: forecast errors that occasionally ruin a day (not just nudge an average) argue for RMSE's outlier sensitivity.

prompt: 'Data drift' in a deployed model means…

options.text: …the input distribution has shifted from what the model trained on (new formats, segments, behaviors), degrading performance even though the code is unchanged
…the database is physically moving
…the model's weights decay over time
…users forget how to use the product

explanation: The world moves; the model's snapshot doesn't. Monitoring input stats and quality proxies (correction rates) is the early-warning system.
